title: Performance Optimization Guidelines
数据库查询优化
content:
优化数据库查询以提升应用性能。

## 关键策略
- 警惕 N+1 查询问题：使用 eager loading (JOIN) 替代 lazy loading
- 为常用的查询条件建立适当的索引
- 使用 EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE 分析查询计划
- 避免在 WHERE 子句中对列使用函数（会使索引失效）
- 批量操作时使用批处理（batch insert/update），而非逐条操作
- 对大型数据集使用分页（cursor-based 优于 offset-based）

title: 缓存策略
content:
合理使用缓存减少重复计算和 I/O。

## 缓存层次
- 应用层缓存：内存缓存（dict, lru_cache）适合热点数据
- 分布式缓存：Redis/Memcached 适合多实例共享
- HTTP 缓存：设置 Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified 头
- CDN 缓存：静态资源使用 CDN 并设置长期缓存

## 注意事项
- 实施缓存失效策略（TTL, 事件驱动的失效）
- 避免缓存穿透（查询不存在的数据）、缓存击穿（热点 key 过期）
- 监控缓存命中率，低于 80% 需要重新评估策略

title: Don't optimize without reason
content:
##### Reason

title: Don't optimize something that's not performance critical
content: ##### Reason Optimizing a non-performance-critical part of a program has no effect on system performance. If your program spends most of its time waiting for the web or for a human, optimization of in-memory computation is probably useless. Put another way: If your program spends 4% of its processing time doing computation A and 40% of its time doing computation B, a 50% improvement on A is only as impactful as a 5% improvement on B. (If you don't even know how much time is spent on A or B, see Per.1 and Per.2.)

title: Don't assume that complicated code is necessarily faster than simple code

title: Don't make claims about performance without measurements
content:
##### Reason
The field of performance is littered with myth and bogus folklore.
Modern hardware and optimizers defy naive assumptions; even experts are regularly surprised.
Getting good performance measurements can be hard and require specialized tools.
A few simple microbenchmarks using Unix time or the standard-library <chrono> can help dispel the most obvious myths.
If you can't measure your complete system accurately, at least try to measure a few of your key operations and algorithms.
A profiler can help tell you which parts of your system are performance critical.
Often, you will be surprised.

title: Design to enable optimization
content:
##### Reason
Because we often need to optimize the initial design.
Because a design that ignores the possibility of later improvement is hard to change.
Premature optimization is said to be [the root of all evil](#rper-knuth), but that's not a reason to despise performance.
It is never premature to consider what makes a design amenable to improvement, and improved performance is a commonly desired improvement.
Aim to build a set of habits that by default results in efficient, maintainable, and optimizable code.
In particular, when you write a function that is not a one-off implementation detail, consider
* Information passing:
Prefer clean [interfaces](#s-interfaces) carrying sufficient information for later improvement of implementation.
Note that information flows into and out of an implementation through the interfaces we provide.
* Compact data: By default, [use compact data](#rper-compact), such as std::vector and [access it in a systematic fashion](#rper-access).
If you think you need a linked structure, try to craft the interface so that this structure isn't seen by users.
* Function argument passing and return:
Distinguish between mutable and non-mutable data.
Don't impose a resource management burden on your users.
Don't impose spurious run-time indirections on your users.
Use [conventional ways](#rf-conventional) of passing information through an interface;
unconventional and/or "optimized" ways of passing data can seriously complicate later reimplementation.
* Abstraction:
Don't overgeneralize; a design that tries to cater for every possible use (and misuse) and defers every design decision for later
(using compile-time or run-time indirections) is usually a complicated, bloated, hard-to-understand mess.
Generalize from concrete examples, preserving performance as we generalize.
Do not generalize based on mere speculation about future needs.
The ideal is zero-overhead generalization.
* Libraries:
Use libraries with good interfaces.
If no library is available build one yourself and imitate the interface style from a good library.
The [standard library](#sl-the-standard-library) is a good first place to look for inspiration.
* Isolation:
Isolate your code from messy and/or old-style code by providing an interface of your choosing to it.
This is sometimes called "providing a wrapper" for the useful/necessary but messy code.
Don't let bad designs "bleed into" your code.
Do not simply craft the interface to match the first implementation and the first use case you think of.
Once your first initial implementation is complete, review it; once you deploy it, mistakes will be hard to remedy.
A need for efficiency does not imply a need for [low-level code](#rper-low).
High-level code isn't necessarily slow or bloated.
Things have costs.
Don't be paranoid about costs (modern computers really are very fast),
but have a rough idea of the order of magnitude of cost of what you use.
For example, have a rough idea of the cost of
a memory access,
a function call,
a string comparison,
a system call,
a disk access,
and a message through a network.
If you can only think of one implementation, you probably don't have something for which you can devise a stable interface.
Maybe, it is just an implementation detail - not every piece of code needs a stable interface - but pause and consider.
One question that can be useful is
"what interface would be needed if this operation should be implemented using multiple threads? be vectorized?"
This rule does not contradict the [Don't optimize prematurely](#rper-knuth) rule.
It complements it, encouraging developers to enable later - appropriate and non-premature - optimization, if and where needed.

title: Rely on the static type system
content:
##### Reason
Type violations, weak types (e.g. void*s), and low-level code (e.g., manipulation of sequences as individual bytes) make the job of the optimizer much harder. Simple code often optimizes better than hand-crafted complex code.
???

title: Move computation from run time to compile time
content:
##### Reason
To decrease code size and run time.
To avoid data races by using constants.
To catch errors at compile time (and thus eliminate the need for error-handling code).
The ideal is *not* to try to execute everything at compile time.
Obviously, most computations depend on inputs, so they can't be moved to compile time,
but beyond that logical constraint is the fact that complex compile-time computation can seriously increase compile times
and complicate debugging.
It is even possible to slow down code by compile-time computation.
This is admittedly rare, but by factoring out a general computation into separate optimal sub-calculations, it is possible to render the instruction cache less effective.

title: Avoid context switches on the critical path
content: ??? # CP: Concurrency and parallelism We often want our computers to do many tasks at the same time (or at least appear to do them at the same time). The reasons for doing so vary (e.g., waiting for many events using only a single processor, processing many data streams simultaneously, or utilizing many hardware facilities) and so do the basic facilities for expressing concurrency and parallelism. Here, we articulate principles and rules for using the ISO standard C++ facilities for expressing basic concurrency and parallelism. Threads are the machine-level foundation for concurrent and parallel programming. Threads allow running multiple sections of a program independently, while sharing the same memory. Concurrent programming is tricky, because protecting shared data between threads is easier said than done. Making existing single-threaded code execute concurrently can be as trivial as adding std::async or std::thread strategically, or it can necessitate a full rewrite, depending on whether the original code was written in a thread-friendly way. The concurrency/parallelism rules in this document are designed with three goals in mind: * To help in writing code that is amenable to being used in a threaded environment * To show clean, safe ways to use the threading primitives offered by the standard library * To offer guidance on what to do when concurrency and parallelism aren't giving the performance gains needed It is also important to note that concurrency in C++ is an unfinished story. C++11 introduced many core concurrency primitives, C++14 and C++17 improved on them, and there is much interest in making the writing of concurrent programs in C++ even easier. We expect some of the library-related guidance here to change significantly over time. This section needs a lot of work (obviously). Please note that we start with rules for relative non-experts. Real experts must wait a bit; contributions are welcome, but please think about the majority of programmers who are struggling to get their concurrent programs correct and performant. Concurrency and parallelism rule summary: * [CP.1: Assume that your code will run as part of a multi-threaded program](#rconc-multi) * [CP.2: Avoid data races](#rconc-races) * [CP.3: Minimize explicit sharing of writable data](#rconc-data) * [CP.4: Think in terms of tasks, rather than threads](#rconc-task) * [CP.8: Don't try to use volatile for synchronization](#rconc-volatile) * [CP.9: Whenever feasible use tools to validate your concurrent code](#rconc-tools) **See also**: * [CP.con: Concurrency](#sscp-con) * [CP.coro: Coroutines](#sscp-coro) * [CP.par: Parallelism](#sscp-par) * [CP.mess: Message passing](#sscp-mess) * [CP.vec: Vectorization](#sscp-vec) * [CP.free: Lock-free programming](#sscp-free) * [CP.etc: Etc. concurrency rules](#sscp-etc)

title: Amdahl's Law
content: > Amdahl's Law is a formula which shows the _potential speedup_ of a computational task which can be achieved by increasing the resources of a system. Normally used in parallel computing, it can predict the actual benefit of increasing the number of processors, which is limited by the parallelisability of the program. Best illustrated with an example. If a program is made up of two parts, part A, which must be executed by a single processor, and part B, which can be parallelised, then we see that adding multiple processors to the system executing the program can only have a limited benefit. It can potentially greatly improve the speed of part B - but the speed of part A will remain unchanged. The diagram below shows some examples of potential improvements in speed: As can be seen, even a program which is 50% parallelisable will benefit very little beyond 10 processing units, whereas a program which is 95% parallelisable can still achieve significant speed improvements with over a thousand processing units. As [Moore's Law](#moores-law) slows, and the acceleration of individual processor speed slows, parallelisation is key to improving performance. Graphics programming is an excellent example - with modern Shader based computing, individual pixels or fragments can be rendered in parallel - this is why modern graphics cards often have many thousands of processing cores (GPUs or Shader Units). See also: - [Brooks' Law](#brooks-law) - [Moore's Law](#moores-law)

title: Performance Investigation Methodology
content:
You are an expert in performance investigation methodology.

## Investigation Principles
- Measure before optimizing; never guess at bottlenecks
- Profile in a production-like environment with realistic workloads
- Isolate the bottleneck layer (CPU, memory, I/O, network, lock contention)
- Change one variable at a time and re-measure

## Bottleneck Identification
- Start with high-level system metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network)
- Drill down to process-level, then thread-level, then code-level
- Use flame graphs and profiling tools (perf, py-spy, pprof, Xcode Instruments)
- Trace request latency through each service boundary
- Identify the slowest percentile (p50, p95, p99) and the critical path

## Capacity Assessment
- Measure current utilization under peak and typical load
- Identify the first resource to saturate (bottleneck)
- Model headroom: how much growth before saturation?
- Test burst scenarios and recovery behavior
- Document scaling limits and recommended thresholds

## Optimization Validation
- Establish a before/after benchmark with statistical significance
- Verify optimization actually improves the identified bottleneck
- Check for regression in non-targeted paths
- Document the expected improvement, actual improvement, and tradeoffs

Profile first, identify the actual bottleneck, fix it, measure again. title: FEC-PERF: Optimize images for performance 优化图片性能
content: Optimize images: (1) Use modern formats: WebP (lossy/lossless) and AVIF (30% better than WebP). (2) Serve responsive images with 'srcset' and 'sizes'. (3) Compress: quality 80-85% for photos (lossy), PNG for graphics requiring transparency. (4) Lazy load below-fold images with 'loading="lazy"'. (5) Use 'fetchpriority="high"' for LCP image. (6) Use CDN with image transformation capabilities (Imgix, Cloudinary, Next.js Image). (7) Implement image placeholders (blur-up, dominant color, or LQIP). Images are typically 60-70% of page weight — optimizing them has outsized impact.

title: FEC-PERF: Optimize webfont loading 优化Web字体加载
content: Optimize webfont loading: (1) Use 'font-display: swap' (or optional) to prevent invisible text during load. (2) Self-host fonts (reduce DNS lookups and improve cache control). (3) Subset fonts to include only needed characters. (4) Preload fonts: '<link rel="preload" href="font.woff2" as="font" crossorigin>'. (5) Use WOFF2 format (30-50% smaller than WOFF). (6) Consider variable fonts (single file, multiple weights). (7) Limit font families and weights — each additional weight increases download size. FOUT (Flash of Unstyled Text) is preferable to FOIT (Flash of Invisible Text).

title: FEC-PERF: Use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 使用HTTP/2或HTTP/3
content: Use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for multiplexed connections: (1) HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over a single TCP connection — eliminates head-of-line blocking. (2) Server push (use with caution, mostly unnecessary with good HTML). (3) HTTP/3 uses QUIC (UDP-based) for even faster connection establishment. (4) Enable on your CDN and web server (nginx: http2, Caddy: automatic). (5) Health check: verify in Chrome DevTools Network tab (h2 or h3 protocol). (6) HTTP/2 eliminates the need for domain sharding, image spriting, and CSS sprites — undo those optimizations. HTTP/2 gives ~15-50% performance improvement over HTTP/1.1 for multi-resource pages.

title: FEC-SEO: Implement proper meta tags 实施正确的Meta标签
content: Implement essential meta tags: (1) Title: '<title>Primary Keyword — Site Name</title>' (50-60 chars). (2) Meta description: '<meta name="description" content="...">' (150-160 chars, includes keywords). (3) Open Graph tags for social sharing: 'og:title', 'og:description', 'og:image', 'og:url'. (4) Twitter Cards: 'twitter:card', 'twitter:title', 'twitter:description', 'twitter:image'. (5) Viewport: '<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">'. (6) Canonical URL: '<link rel="canonical" href="...">' to prevent duplicate content. Meta tags are critical for search ranking, social sharing previews, and mobile rendering.

title: FEC-SEO: Implement structured data (JSON-LD) 实施结构化数据
content: Implement JSON-LD structured data for rich search results. Common schemas: (1) Article/BlogPosting — news, blog posts. (2) Product — e-commerce (price, availability, reviews). (3) LocalBusiness — local SEO (address, phone, hours). (4) FAQPage — frequently asked questions (expandable in search). (5) BreadcrumbList — site navigation path. (6) Review — product/service reviews with ratings. (7) Event — dates, location, ticket info. Test with Google's Rich Results Test. Structured data can significantly improve CTR from search results.

title: FEC-SEO: Implement XML sitemap and robots.txt 实施站点地图和robots.txt
content: Implement: (1) XML Sitemap at '/sitemap.xml' listing all important pages with lastmod, changefreq, priority. Submit to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. (2) robots.txt at '/robots.txt' with: User-agent directives, Disallow rules for private/admin paths, Sitemap link: 'Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml'. (3) Consider separate image/video sitemaps. (4) Use 'noindex' meta tag for pages that shouldn't be indexed (thank-you pages, internal tools, paginated filters). These are foundational SEO: sitemaps help discovery, robots.txt controls crawl budget.

title: FEC-ACCESS: Implement proper heading hierarchy 实施正确的标题层级
content: Ensure heading hierarchy: (1) One '<h1>' per page (page title/topic). (2) Sections use '<h2>', subsections '<h3>', etc. — never skip levels (h1 to h3 without h2). (3) Headings should be descriptive, not generic ('Setup Guide' not 'Click Here'). (4) Use headings for document structure, not for visual styling (use CSS for that). (5) Screen reader users navigate by headings — a good heading outline is like a table of contents. Test: use the Headings extension or WAVE tool to check heading hierarchy.

title: FEC-ACCESS: Implement ARIA landmarks 实施ARIA地标
content: Use ARIA landmark roles to define page regions: 'role="banner"' (site header), 'role="navigation"' (nav), 'role="main"' (main content), 'role="complementary"' (aside), 'role="contentinfo"' (footer), 'role="search"' (search). HTML5 semantic elements (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer>) implicitly map to these roles. Use 'aria-label' for distinguishing multiple landmarks of the same type (e.g., two '<nav>' elements). Landmarks enable screen reader users to jump between page sections efficiently.

title: FEC-ACCESS: Ensure proper color contrast 确保色彩对比度
content: Ensure color contrast ratios meet WCAG 2.1 AA standards: (1) Normal text (<18pt): minimum contrast ratio 4.5:1. (2) Large text (>=18pt or >=14pt bold): minimum 3:1. (3) UI components and graphical objects: minimum 3:1. (4) Focus indicators: minimum 3:1 against adjacent colors. Use tools: WebAIM Contrast Checker, axe DevTools, or Lighthouse. Don't rely on color alone to convey information (use icons + text as well). Test with color blindness simulators (Chrome DevTools rendering tab).

title: FEC-ACCESS: Support keyboard navigation 支持键盘导航
content: Ensure full keyboard navigation: (1) All interactive elements are reachable via Tab. (2) Visible focus indicators on all interactive elements (:focus-visible). (3) Logical tab order matching visual layout. (4) No keyboard traps (focus can Tab out of any element). (5) Custom components have correct ARIA roles and keyboard handlers (Enter/Space for activation, Arrow keys for list navigation, Escape for closing). (6) Skip navigation link: 'Skip to main content' as first focusable element. Test: navigate the entire application using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape only.
